cues.text: A Young Deacon at Nicaea
Born around the year 296 in Alexandria, Athanasius received an excellent education and was ordained deacon while still young, becoming the close and trusted secretary of his bishop, Alexander.
In this capacity, he accompanied Alexander to the great Council of Nicaea in 325.
Though not yet a bishop and therefore without a vote, his sharp theological mind is widely believed to have shaped the council’s crucial defense of the Son’s full divinity against Arius’s teaching.
Within three years, on Alexander's death, the clergy and people of Alexandria acclaimed the young Athanasius as their new bishop.
Though he could not have known it then, this choice would commit him to nearly half a century of unrelenting struggle in defense of the very faith he had helped articulate at Nicaea.
Exiled Again and Again
The condemnation of Arius at Nicaea did not end the controversy; it merely drove it underground, where it found powerful friends at the imperial court.
Athanasius refused every pressure to compromise or even soften the Nicene formula for the sake of a false peace.

He was deposed on trumped-up charges and exiled by the Emperor Constantine himself in 335 — the first of what would become five separate exiles , spanning altogether some seventeen years of his forty-five-year episcopate.
Each time a more favorable political wind allowed his return, Athanasius came back to Alexandria, not embittered but undiminished in resolve.
Yet he was driven out again as theological and political tides shifted once more against him—a pattern of suffering and endurance that would have broken a lesser man's spirit many times over.
Alone Against an Empire
By the middle of the fourth century, successive emperors favored Arian or semi-Arian formulas.
One council after another produced compromises that watered down the Nicene confession.
For a time, it could genuinely seem that the whole visible Church had drifted from the faith Athanasius had defended since his youth.
It is from this bleak period that history has preserved the phrase that best captures his lonely fidelity: Athanasius contra mundum — Athanasius against the world.
We should not read in this phrase despair, but rather the deepest kind of hope: the conviction that truth does not depend on numbers.
Athanasius never abandoned this conviction, even when nearly every other bishop of standing had bent to imperial pressure.
One faithful witness, sustained by grace, can outlast an empire's worth of compromise.
A Friend of the Desert Monks
During his periods of exile, Athanasius often found refuge among the monks of the Egyptian desert, the spiritual sons of St. Anthony .
Their friendship and protection sheltered him through his most dangerous years.
He came to know their way of life intimately.
Out of this friendship came his Life of Anthony , a work that would do more than perhaps any other single book to spread the monastic ideal across the Christian world, East and West alike.
Athanasius also gave the Church another gift of lasting importance.
In his Easter letter of 367, he became the first writer we know of to list the twenty-seven books of the New Testament exactly as the Church recognizes them today.
This was a quiet but immensely consequential act of pastoral care for the flock he had defended his whole life.
Vindication at Last
Athanasius lived to see the tide of the controversy at last begin turning decisively in favor of the Nicene faith he had never abandoned.
This came only in his final years, aided by the theological labors of the younger Cappadocian Fathers, who built carefully on the foundation he had defended almost single-handedly for so long.
He died in Alexandria in 373, restored at last to his own see.
He had spent nearly seventeen of his forty-five years as bishop in exile for the sake of one precisely chosen word: homoousios , of one substance with the Father.
Legacy
Eight years after his death, the Council of Constantinople in 381 completed and confirmed the confession Athanasius had spent his life defending.
The Nicene-Constantinopolitan Creed that Catholics recite at Mass every Sunday still reflects the Nicene faith he defended.
He teaches every generation of believers that fidelity to revealed truth may, at times, require standing entirely alone.
Such solitary faithfulness, far from being fruitless, can in the end preserve for the whole Church a treasure that no passing consensus of the age could be trusted to keep safe.
